newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe may raise interest rates to cut inflation.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe may raise interest rates to cut inflation.

text.p: Zimbabwe's central bank governor said he could be forced to raise interest rates to beat resurgent inflation which is undermining the southern African nation's economic recovery.

In an interview with Reuters, Leonard Tsumba, the governor of Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ), said there had been a steady increase in annual inflation in the last five months after it had dropped to a seven-year low of 13.8 percent last November.
In the year to April annual inflation rose to a 10-month high of 22.4 percent from 19.9 percent in March, raising fears that this year's average will surpass last year's 21.7 percent.
Tsumba blamed the rise partly on money supply growth, which has averaged over 30 percent monthly in the past few months against a monthly average target of 22 percent.
He said the central bank was working on a programme to bring both inflation and money supply growth down, but he gave no details.
Asked whether this would include raising the official rediscount rate currently pegged at 23.5 percent, he said:
"That is one option but we are still assessing the situation. But there are also other things we can do.
"Part of our problem is that the economy, although it has been growing remains very fragile. But we have to establish a trend where the inflation must go down," he said.

Zimbabwe's agriculture-powered economy grew by about eight percent in 1996, and Tsumba told Reuters he expects real growth rate to be about five percent this year compared to an agriculture-propelled eight percent rise in 1996.
"We are expecting a five percent growth in real terms this year. Last year's (growth rate) was after hitting a trough," he said.
Over the last 10 years, gross domestic product (GDP) growth has averaged less than one percent annually in the face of intermittent droughts.
"Part of the (inflation) problem is also a result of money supply growth," he said.
Tsumba said he expected the new efforts to help bring down annual inflation, initially targeted to fall to around 17 percent by June this year, to around 20 percent by the end of the year.
"The objective is also to bring down money supply growth to a 22 percent range," the RBZ governor said.

Short-term interest rates on Zimbabwe's money market have risen from around 16 percent last month to range between 24 and 25 percent on fears a recent bout of price increases will feed annual inflation.
